items.title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.publisher: Financial Reporting Council
items.locator: Provisions 25 and 26 (pages 12-13 of the document); Provision 29
items.quote: where there is no internal audit function, an explanation for the absence, how internal assurance is achieved
items.why: The governance rule on assurance for companies that follow the Code, on a comply or explain basis. The audit committee monitors and reviews the effectiveness of internal audit or, where there is none, considers each year whether one is needed; the annual report explains how internal assurance is achieved without one. Not specific to AI. Provision 29 (board review and declaration on material controls) applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2026.

items.title: Introduction to AI assurance
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section on roles in the assurance ecosystem (accreditation bodies; UKAS); sections 5.2 (assurance spectrum), 5.6 (bias audit), 5.7 (compliance audit), 5.8 (conformity assessment)
items.quote: Contingent on the level of risk, conformity assessment activities should be undertaken by an independent third-party conformity assessment body.
items.why: Government's plain guide to what assurance is and who provides it. Sets out the techniques, ties the need for an independent third party to the level of risk, names ISO/IEC 42001 as a standard to measure against, and states government policy that third-party conformity assessment should come from a body accredited by the national accreditation service.

items.title: Assuring a responsible future for AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Executive summary ('Our research has found'); section 'Opportunities for future market growth' (supply; public research finding)
items.quote: Participants felt that, if assurance were delivered only by an AI developer that is profit motivated, it would not be trustworthy.
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation and of the figure. Government's first survey of the UK AI assurance market: an estimated 524 firms supplying assurance goods and services, 84 of them specialised, generating an estimated £1.01 billion. Reports that developers are the largest group of assurance providers and that the public regard who assures as mattering as much as how.

items.title: Trusted third-party AI assurance roadmap
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section 'Challenges for a trusted third-party assurance market' (Quality; Skills; Information access); 'Government actions' (professionalisation)
items.quote: the quality of the goods and services provided is currently unclear
items.why: The caution a board needs before relying on bought assurance. Government says the quality of AI assurance services is unclear, existing certifications of AI assurance competence are hard to judge and none is issued by an accredited organisation, technical standards are still developing, and providers lack access to information about systems. Sets out plans for an AI assurance profession.

items.title: Portfolio of AI assurance techniques
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Sections 'About the portfolio' and 'Assurance techniques'
items.quote: the inclusion of a case study in the portfolio does not represent a government endorsement of the technique or the organisation
items.why: A searchable set of case studies of assurance in use: impact assessment, impact evaluation, bias audit, compliance audit, certification, conformity assessment, performance testing and formal verification. Useful for scoping a review. The page says inclusion is not an endorsement.

items.title: Global Internal Audit Standards
items.publisher: The Institute of Internal Auditors
items.locator: Principle 7 ('Positioned Independently'); Standard 8.4 ('External Quality Assessment'); Glossary, 'independence'
items.quote: The external assessment must be performed at least once every five years by a qualified, independent assessor or assessment team.
items.why: The profession's definition of independence and its own rule on being checked. Independence is freedom from conditions that impair the function's ability to act without bias; the chief audit executive reports to the board; the function itself is externally assessed at least every five years. Free copy marked for individual personal use.

items.title: The IIA's Artificial Intelligence Auditing Framework
items.publisher: The Institute of Internal Auditors
items.locator: Part 3 ('AI Auditing Framework'), opening section and 'Governance' (document page 11-12); Part 2 (right to audit clause for vendors, page 10)
items.quote: internal audit likely will be able to provide only limited assurance
items.why: How internal audit is expected to approach AI as the third line: advising, and giving assurance on the processes and controls management has set up. Candid about limits: because AI is complex and changing, internal audit is likely to give only limited assurance. Copyright 2024; the file name dates the update to September 2024, no date is printed on the cover.

items.title: ISO/IEC 42001 - AI Management System
items.publisher: BSI Group
items.locator: Introductory section and FAQs ('What is BSI’s experience in auditing AI Management Systems?')
items.quote: BSI is the first Certification Body accredited by UKAS to certify ISO/IEC 42001
items.why: Evidence that accredited certification of an AI management system is available in the UK. This is a certification body's own sales page, so the claim about being first is its own. The standard itself is paid for and ISO's free pages for ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO/IEC 42006 refused the request in this pass, so neither is cited. Undated page; read 2 October 2026.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 146: Assessment notices
items.publisher: legislation.gov.uk
items.quote: to carry out an assessment of whether the controller or processor has complied or is complying with the data protection legislation
items.why: The compulsory form of outside review. The regulator may by notice require a controller or processor to permit an assessment of its data protection compliance, including entry to premises and inspection of documents and equipment. It reaches AI only so far as personal data is processed. The text now reads 'the Commission'.

items.title: Data protection audit framework
items.publisher: Information Commissioner's Office
items.locator: Introductory text; under-review banner; link to the artificial intelligence toolkit
items.quote: using our audit toolkits to conduct both consensual and compulsory audits
items.why: The regulator publishes the toolkits its auditors use, including one on artificial intelligence, so an organisation can see what an outside reviewer would test. The page says following it does not guarantee compliance and carries a banner that the guidance is under review because of the Data (Use and Access) Act. Page metadata date 10 September 2025.

items.title: SS1/23: Model risk management principles for banks
items.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
items.locator: Principle 4 ('Independent model validation') and Principle 4.1 (the independent validation function); Principle 2.5 (Internal Audit); para 1.5 (in effect 17 May 2024)
items.quote: Firms should have a validation process that provides ongoing, independent, and effective challenge to model development and use.
items.why: The clearest UK supervisory expectation of independent review of models, AI models included. Banks should have a validation function giving an objective, unbiased and critical opinion, and internal audit should periodically assess the effectiveness of the whole model risk framework. Applies to banks, building societies and PRA-designated investment firms with internal model approval; a benchmark elsewhere, not a rule. A supervisory statement of expectations, in effect from 17 May 2024.

items.title: AI Act, Article 43: Conformity assessment (AI Act Service Desk copy)
items.publisher: European Commission
items.locator: Article 43(1) and (2), paragraph 2 marked AMENDED; Commission summary at the head of the page
items.quote: based on internal control as referred to in Annex VI, which does not provide for the involvement of a notified body
items.why: The Commission's own copy, not the Official Journal; it says the text follows the EUR-Lex consolidated version of the AI Act as at 27 July 2026 and marks Digital Omnibus changes. Shows how limited compulsory third-party review is even under the EU Act: for the high-risk uses in points 2 to 8 of Annex III (employment, credit, education and others) the provider assesses its own conformity by internal control, with no independent notified body; a notified body is involved for biometrics in defined cases and for AI in regulated products. A duty on providers, not deployers; high-risk rules are not yet in application.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Section 5.3 (Measure), introductory text, document page 28; Table 3, MEASURE 1.3
items.quote: Processes for independent review can improve the effectiveness of testing and can mitigate internal biases
items.why: International comparator. A voluntary United States framework that builds independence into measurement: MEASURE 1.3 asks that internal experts who were not front-line developers, or independent assessors, take part in regular assessments. Supports the brief's point that the reviewer should be independent of those who built or run the system. Voluntary; no audit or certification scheme attaches to it.

items.title: Notice of Adoption of Final Rule: Use of Automated Employment Decision Tools (6 RCNY Chapter 5, Subchapter T)
items.publisher: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
items.locator: Section 5-300, definition of 'Independent auditor'; section 5-301(a) (bias audit within the past year)
items.quote: a person or group that is capable of exercising objective and impartial judgment on all issues within the scope of a bias audit
items.why: International comparator: a rare example of law that compels an independent audit of an AI system. An employer in New York City may not use an automated hiring tool unless it has had a bias audit in the past year by an independent auditor, defined to exclude anyone involved in using, developing or distributing the tool. A city rule covering hiring and promotion tools and bias only; it has no force in the UK and says nothing of governance more widely. The notice prints no adoption date; the year is taken from its hearing dates (January 2023) and the file path (April 2023).

items.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
items.publisher: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), published by The National Archives
items.locator: Paragraph 199 (Ground 5, public sector equality duty); paragraph 201
items.quote: either directly or by way of independent verification, that the software program in this case does not have an unacceptable bias
items.why: A UK court treating independent verification as part of what a reasonable deployer does. The police force had never sought to satisfy itself, directly or by independent verification, that its facial recognition software was free of unacceptable race or sex bias, and so had not done all it reasonably could to meet the public sector equality duty. Applies to public authorities under the Equality Act 2010 section 149; it does not create a general duty to commission an audit.

items.title: Ensuring statistical models command public confidence: learning lessons from the approach to developing models for awarding grades in the UK in 2020
items.publisher: Office for Statistics Regulation
items.locator: Section 3.4.1.1 ('Engagement with commissioners of the model and others who can help ensure the results meet the need'); section 3.3.1.1 (external challenge through Red Teams or independent advisory panels)
items.quote: the qualification regulators could have made greater use of opportunities for independent challenge to the overall approach
items.why: An official review of a public algorithm failure, the 2020 exam grading models in all four UK nations. The statistics regulator found that more independent challenge might have helped secure public confidence, and recommends that anyone developing a model fully explore opportunities for it. About statistical models in the public sector in exceptional circumstances; a regulator's review, not a statutory inquiry.

items.title: Government Response: Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme
items.publisher: Australian Government, Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
items.locator: Recommendation 17.2 ('Establishment of a body to monitor and audit automated decision-making') and the Government's response, p.22
items.quote: with the power to monitor and audit automated decision-making processes
items.why: An official inquiry concluding that automated decision-making needs outside audit. The Royal Commission recommended a body with power to monitor and audit automated decision-making for its technical aspects and for fairness, bias and usability; the Australian Government accepted the recommendation. Read in the Government's response, which reproduces the recommendation: the Royal Commission's own site did not respond today. Australian public sector; acceptance is a commitment to consider, not a body in being.

items.title: Outsider Oversight: Designing a Third Party Audit Ecosystem for AI Governance
items.publisher: Inioluwa Deborah Raji, Peggy Xu, Colleen Honigsberg and Daniel E. Ho (arXiv; AAAI/ACM AIES 2022)
items.locator: Abstract (arXiv:2206.04737v1)
items.quote: the turn toward audits alone is unlikely to achieve actual algorithmic accountability
items.why: Peer-reviewed conference paper, read on the authors' arXiv copy. Compares audit regimes in finance, environment and health and concludes that audits alone are unlikely to deliver accountability: what matters is the institutional design around them, including how third parties are able to take part. A review and argument, not new data. Only the abstract is quoted.

items.title: AI auditing: The Broken Bus on the Road to AI Accountability
items.publisher: Abeba Birhane, Ryan Steed, Victor Ojewale, Briana Vecchione and Inioluwa Deborah Raji (arXiv; IEEE SaTML 2024)
items.locator: Abstract (arXiv:2401.14462v1)
items.quote: We find that only a subset of AI audit studies translate to desired accountability outcomes.
items.why: Evidence for the criterion's top level, findings that change practice. The authors classify AI audits done by regulators, law firms, civil society, journalists, academics and consultancies and assess what each achieved; only some led to any change. Supports asking what a review altered, not whether one took place. Accepted conference paper read on arXiv; a review of published audits, so unpublished internal audits are outside it.

items.title: Auditing large language models: a three-layered approach
items.publisher: Jakob Mökander, Jonas Schuett, Hannah Rose Kirk and Luciano Floridi (arXiv; AI and Ethics, 2023)
items.locator: Abstract (arXiv:2302.08500v2)
items.quote: it is important to remain realistic about what auditing can reasonably be expected to achieve
items.why: How to scope a review of generative AI. Proposes three linked audits: of the provider's governance, of the model before release, and of each application built on it. Candid about limits, including whether such models can be audited at all. A journal article read on the authors' arXiv copy; a proposed method, not a tested one.

items.title: The IIA's Three Lines Model: an update of the Three Lines of Defense
items.publisher: The Institute of Internal Auditors
items.locator: Principle 5 ('Third line independence'); Principle 4 ('Third line roles')
items.quote: Internal audit's independence from the responsibilities of management is critical to its objectivity, authority, and credibility.
items.why: The model behind the phrase 'third line'. Sets out what makes assurance independent inside an organisation: accountability to the governing body, unfettered access to people and data, and freedom from bias or interference. Helps a board tell self-review (first and second line) from independent review. A professional body's position paper, not a standard and not about AI; copyright 2020, file marked 'Updated September 2024'.
